changes.before: If this example uses Rc instead of Arc, what happens?
changes.after: Rust checks whether a value can move to another thread. This rule is called Send.

before: Send means a value’s ownership may be transferred between threads; Sync means sharing &T between threads is safe. These are marker traits, usually derived automatically from a type’s contents. Do not write unsafe implementations merely to suppress a compiler error.

The worked value is Arc<i32>, which satisfies the relevant bounds. Replacing Arc with Rc asks thread::spawn to capture a non-Send reference-counted pointer; the compiler rejects that boundary before any thread executes. The correct repair depends on ownership and access needs, not just silencing a diagnostic.
Expected output or behavior: 7. Compiler evidence is recorded separately from app reading completion.

Optional local transfer task: Explain the separate questions of sharing ownership and protecting mutable payloads. You may trace it without a Rust compiler; reading completion is not proof of a local run.
after: Rust checks whether a value can move to another thread. This rule is called Send.
Arc keeps its owner count safe across threads. Rc does not. Sync is the related rule for sharing references across threads.
The output is `7`. The worker can take this Arc and read its number.
Find the value that crosses into the worker thread.

before.question: If this example uses Rc instead of Arc, what happens?
choices: It silently changes Rc reference counts into atomics.
It always runs safely because the inner value is an integer.
Compilation rejects transferring Rc into the spawned thread.
before.explanation: Rc itself lacks Send; a safe inner integer does not repair its non-atomic shared ownership mechanism.

after.question: Would the same program build if it used Rc instead of Arc?
choices: Yes. Every owner can move between threads.
Yes. The worker would just receive zero.
No. This Rc cannot move to the worker thread.
after.explanation: Rc cannot safely move into this new thread. Rust rejects the program before it runs.
